policy_title: Empower local authorities to introduce rent controls and strengthen tenants' rights
stated: Empower local authorities to introduce rent controls, end Section 21 no-fault evictions, introduce long-term leases, give tenants the right to demand energy efficiency improvements, and establish Private Residential Tenancy Boards for dispute resolution.

source.quote: Elected Greens will push to: • Empower local authorities to introduce rent controls. • End no-fault evictions. Rent controls: Elected Greens will give the power to local authorities to control rents if the local rental market is overheated. A new stable rental tenancy and the ending of no-fault evictions: Elected Greens will push to end Section 21 no-fault evictions and introduce long-term leases. Renters will also be given a new right to demand energy efficiency improvements. Private Residential Tenancy Boards: Elected Greens will introduce Private Residential Tenancy Boards.

bearing_set.reason: Rent controls directly target rent-as-%-of-income (a core O1 indicator); security-of-tenure measures (ending S.21, long-term leases) and dispute boards shape whether tenants can maintain stable, affordable housing — but contested supply-side effects on rental stock also earn a real verdict here.

The explicit right for tenants to demand energy efficiency improvements maps directly onto the energy bills indicator: better-insulated rental homes lower energy costs for households in the UK's least energy-efficient housing tenure.
The right to demand energy-efficiency improvements directly targets building-level energy consumption and emissions, a non-negligible effect on the UK's building-stock emissions trajectory.

Rent controls and mandatory lease/eviction terms restrict landlords' freedom to price and manage their own property — a concrete constraint on property rights, which are explicitly within O10's scope.

The package transfers economic value from landlords (a population with substantially higher average wealth) to tenants (lower average wealth), concretely narrowing the income/wealth gap and bearing on inequality indicators.

membership_note: Four fundamentals are warranted: O1 is the primary target; O6 is a direct environmental mechanism (energy-efficiency clause); O10 captures the property-rights cost imposed on landlords; O14 captures the redistributive transfer from a wealthier to a less-wealthy group. Fiscal effects (tenancy boards) are too small to clear the O12 non-negligible bar. O13 supply-side concern (landlords exiting market) is real but sits within the O1 mixed verdict rather than a distinct aggregate-prosperity mechanism.
